source_text: Λέγω τοίνυν αὖθις ἃ καὶ πρότερον εἴρηκα, πάνυ ματαίως ἀνθρώπους διακεῖσθαι, καὶ μήτε ὑπερβολὴν ὅλως ἐνδέχεσθαι τῶν ἐπινοουμένων πραγμάτων τὴν ματαιότητα. Περιττὸς δέ μοι ὁ κάματος ἐκκλησιάζοντι σοφῶς, ὅτι διδάσκειν ἐπιχειρῶν τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον ἀδιδάκτως καὶ ἀνιάτως ἔχοντα. Δεῖ δὲ ἀνδρὸς γενναίου, πρὸς τὸ συνιέναι λόγους σοφίας δυνηθῆναι. Ἐγὼ δὲ ἤδη πρεσβύτης ὢν, καὶ μακρὸν βίου διελθὼν χρόνον, ἔκαμον εἰς τὸ ἀνευρεῖν τὰ τῷ Θεῷ ἀρεστὰ διὰ τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας μυστηρίων. Ἐπίσταμαί τε ὡς ἐπεγείρει ψυχὰς, καὶ νύττει οὐχ ἧττον τὰ τῶν σοφῶν παραγγέλματα, ἢ διατίθεται σώματα βουκέντρῳ, ἢ ἥλῳ ἐμπερονηθέντα. Δώσουσι δέ τινες τὰ σοφὰ ἐκεῖνα διδάγματα, παρ᾽ ἑνὸς ἀγαθοῦ λαβόντες ποιμένος καὶ διδασκάλου, ὥσπερ ἐξ ἑνὸς στόματος ἅπαντες αὑτοῖς συμφώνως δαψιλέστερον τὰ πιστευθέντα διηγούμενοι. Λόγων δὲ πολλῶν οὐδὲν ὄφελος· οὐδέ σοι συμβουλεύω, ὦ φίλος, ἀνόνητα καταγράφειν τὰ περὶ τὸ προσῆκον, ἐν οἷς τοῦ κάμνειν εἰκῆ ἐστὶν οὐδὲν πλέον. Ἀλλά μοι λοιπὸν ἐπιλόγου δεήσει τοιοῦδέ τινος, ὅτι· Ὦ ἄνθρωποι, ἰδοὺ διαῤῥήδην ὑμῖν καὶ συντόμως προαγορεύω, φοβεῖσθαι μὲν Θεὸν τὸν πάντων δεσπότην τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ἐπόπτην, τηρεῖν δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ παραγγέλματα· πείθεσθαι δὲ, πάντα τινὰ μετέπειτα καὶ κριθήσεσθαι, καὶ κατ᾽ ἀξίαν ἀπολήψεσθαι ἔκαστον τῶν αὑτοῦ ἔργων τὴν ἀμοιβὴν ἀγαθῶν τε ὁμοῦ καὶ φαύλων.
thought_title: Gregory's concluding confession of weariness and final admonition to fear God
orientation: Gregory Thaumaturgus speaks in his own voice as an old man, reiterating the emptiness of human affairs, confessing the toil of teaching an unteachable people, and delivering a final charge to fear God and keep his commandments because all works will be judged.
pass_a_gloss: I say therefore again what I also said before, that human beings are disposed in utter futility, and that no excess whatsoever is possible for the futility of the things devised. The toil is superfluous for me addressing the Church wisely, because I attempt to teach this people unteachably and incurably holding. A noble man is needed to be able to understand words of wisdom. But I, already being an old man, and having passed through a long time of life, toiled to find out the things pleasing to God through the mysteries of truth. I know also that the commands of the wise rouse souls and sting no less than bodies are disposed with a goad, or bodies pierced by a nail. Some will give those wise teachings, having received them from one good shepherd and teacher, as if from one mouth all harmoniously narrate the things believed more abundantly. Of many words there is no profit; nor do I advise you, O friend, to write down useless things concerning what is fitting, in which to toil in vain is nothing more. But a conclusion of such a kind will be needed for me: O human beings, behold I proclaim to you plainly and briefly, to fear God the master of all and overseer together, and to keep also his commandments; to be persuaded that everyone will afterward be judged, and each will receive according to worth the recompense of his own works, both good and worthless together.

lemmas.gloss: address the Church, convene an assembly

choices.why: The Greek repeats the same root (ματ-) for the human disposition and the quality of things devised; 'futility' keeps the lexical link without importing the metaphor of 'vanity' or the banned 'empty and useless'.
περιττός means 'superfluous, beyond what is needed'; 'superfluous' captures the exact sense that the labor exceeds any useful purpose, whereas 'vain' would blur the distinction from ματαίως.
ἐκκλησιάζω is the verb for convening or addressing the ἐκκλησία; the Work Brief fixes 'Church' for Ἐκκλησία, so the participle must carry that sense. 'Wisely' modifies the manner of addressing.
Both are adverbs in -ως describing how the people 'hold' (ἔχοντα); 'unteachably' renders ἀδιδάκτως literally, 'incurably' renders ἀνιάτως (used of diseases), preserving the medical metaphor.

choices.english: with a goad / pierced by the sun
choices.why: βουκέντρον is a cattle-goad; ἐμπεροναέω means 'pierce through'. The simile compares the sting of wise commands to two physical pains: goading bodies and bodies transfixed by the sun's heat. 'Pierced by the sun' keeps the perfect participle's state.

choices.english: narrate the things believed more abundantly
choices.why: δαψιλέστερον is comparative 'more abundantly/copiously'; it modifies how they narrate (διηγούμενοι) what was believed (τὰ πιστευθέντα). 'More abundantly' preserves the comparative force.
Direct address to a single listener/reader; 'friend' is the standard vocative for φίλος. The Brief does not gloss this term, so literal rendering applies.

choices.english: master of all and overseer together
choices.why: δεσπότης = master/lord; ἐπόπτης = overseer/guardian; ὁμοῦ καὶ links them as simultaneous roles. 'Overseer together' renders ἐπόπτην with ὁμοῦ reflected.

bible_refs.note: Fear God and keep his commandments; God will bring every work into judgment, good and evil.
The words of the wise are like goads (βούκεντρα).
Vanity of vanities, all is vanity (ματαιότης).
Of making many books there is no end, and much study is weariness of the flesh (λόγων πολλῶν οὐδὲν ὄφελος).

pass_b_english: Therefore I say again what I said before: human beings conduct themselves in utter futility, and there is no possibility at all that the futility of the things they devise could be exceeded. The toil is superfluous for me as I address the Church wisely, because I try to teach this people who are unteachably and incurably disposed. It takes a noble man to be able to understand words of wisdom. I am already an old man, and I have passed through a long span of life; I have toiled to discover the things pleasing to God through the mysteries of truth. I know that the commands of the wise rouse souls and sting no less than a goad drives bodies, or than bodies pierced by a nail. Some will hand on those wise teachings, having received them from one good shepherd and teacher, so that all of them in accord, as if from one mouth, narrate the things believed more abundantly. Many words bring no profit; nor do I advise you, friend, to write down useless things about what is fitting, in which toiling in vain is nothing more. But I shall need a conclusion something like this: O human beings, behold, I declare to you plainly and briefly: fear God, the master of all and overseer together; keep his commandments too; and be persuaded that everyone will afterward be judged, and each will receive the recompense of his own works according to their worth, both good and worthless together.

problems.quote: or than bodies pierced by the sun
problems.why: ἥλῳ is 'nail' (dative of ἧλος), not the sun. The image is of bodies pierced by a nail, as in Ecclesiastes 12:11 (goads and nails).
problems.fix: or than bodies pierced by a nail.

problems.quote: all things will be examined and judged afterward
problems.why: πάντα τινά means 'everyone' (every person). It does not mean 'all things', and the following clause about each person's works needs a personal subject.
problems.fix: be persuaded that everyone will afterward be judged, and each will receive the recompense of his own works according to their worth.

edits.old: or than bodies pierced by the sun
edits.new: or than bodies pierced by a nail

edits.old: be persuaded that all things will be examined and judged afterward, and each will receive the recompense of his own works according to their worth, both good and worthless together.
edits.new: be persuaded that everyone will afterward be judged, and each will receive the recompense of his own works according to their worth, both good and worthless together.

fixed: 'ἥλῳ' is dative of ἧλος 'nail', not 'sun'; the simile matches Ecclesiastes 12:11 (goads and nails).
'πάντα τινά' means 'everyone' (each person), not 'all things'; the next clause ('each will receive...') requires a personal subject.

last_rejected.quote: narrate the things believed more abundantly
last_rejected.why: τὰ πιστευθέντα means the teachings entrusted to them, not doctrines they believe.
last_rejected.fix: narrate more abundantly the things entrusted to them
last_rejected.ruling: τὰ πιστευθέντα can be rendered 'the things believed'. 'Things entrusted' is a nuance, so the English stays within the word's normal range.

last_rejected.quote: to write down useless things about what is fitting, in which toiling in vain is nothing more
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀνόνητα καταγράφειν τὰ περὶ τὸ προσῆκον, ἐν οἷς τοῦ κάμνειν εἰκῆ ἐστὶν οὐδὲν πλέον
last_rejected.why: ἀνόνητα marks the writing as unprofitable; the clause says those matters yield nothing beyond vain toil.
last_rejected.fix: to write unprofitably about what is fitting, in which there is nothing more than toiling in vain
last_rejected.ruling: ἀνόνητα καταγράφειν is rendered 'write down useless things'. 'Nothing more than toiling in vain' keeps the sense of οὐδὲν πλέον. It is awkward but accurate.
